analysis.one_liner: Bans clearcutting on federal lands and protects old-growth, roadless, and streamside forests from logging.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 134 cosponsors — nearly a third of the House — but never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned clearcutting and other even-aged logging on national forests, Bureau of Land Management land, wildlife refuges, and military lands, requiring loggers to switch to selective cutting that keeps a forest canopy intact. It would have made old-growth forests, roadless areas, stream buffers, and dozens of named special areas off-limits to logging entirely, and it would have let any citizen sue to enforce the rules, including against the federal government itself.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use national forests — hikers, hunters, anglers, campers — plus communities that drink water drawn from forested watersheds, the recreation and fishing businesses that depend on intact forests, and taxpayers, since the bill's own findings state that federal logging programs run at a loss to the Treasury. The bill's findings also argue that selective logging is more labor-intensive than clearcutting, so it would support more logging jobs per unit of timber cut.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits even-aged logging, including clearcutting, seed-tree cutting, and shelterwood cutting, on national forests, public lands, wildlife refuges, and military lands, allowing only selective management that keeps continuous forest cover and native species.
Restricts road construction and logging in Ancient Forests, Roadless Areas, Watershed Protection Areas, and dozens of named Special Areas across 27 states.

Creates a citizen enforcement right: any harmed person can sue violators, including the United States, in any federal district court, with a mandatory minimum $5,000 damage award and attorney fees, and Congress expressly waives the government's sovereign immunity with no notice required.

The bill's findings state that federal logging programs 'are carried out at enormous financial costs to the United States Treasury and American taxpayers,' so ending or reforming them would save public money.
The bill's findings state that selective logging is more job-intensive than clearcutting for the same amount of timber production and produces higher-quality sawlogs.

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies and mills that depend on federal timber sales, particularly those built around clearcutting national forests, would lose access to that supply. Logging towns in the Pacific Northwest and elsewhere would bear the local adjustment costs. Federal agencies would face new citizen lawsuits and mandatory damage awards for management practices the bill outlaws.

drawbacks.text: The bill's definition of even-aged logging is extremely broad — it covers any cutting that removes more than 20 percent of a stand's basal area within 30 years or creates an opening wider than the tallest bordering tree — so it would restrict most conventional timber harvest on federal lands, not just clearcutting, and federal timber supply to mills would shrink sharply.

The citizen-suit provisions are unusually aggressive: mandatory minimum $5,000 statutory damages, fee-shifting, no notice requirement, and a waived sovereign immunity could flood land-management agencies with litigation and shift de facto control of forest decisions toward advocacy groups and the courts.

Existing timber sale contracts are grandfathered — the bill does not apply to contracts awarded before enactment — so the timber industry would keep cutting under old contracts even after the ban took effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most Americans the benefits — cleaner water from protected watersheds, intact old-growth and roadless forests, recreation, and ending below-cost federal logging — outweigh the costs, which fall narrowly and adjustably on the timber industry. The bill's real design problems are procedural rather than substantive: the near-total logging ban defined so broadly, plus mandatory damages and open-ended citizen suits, would hand outsized power to courts and litigants over how public lands are managed. An honest case for the bill depends on accepting that trade-off.

outcome.mechanism: The Speaker sent it to three committees at once, it bounced to four subcommittees, and it sat there from July 1999 until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001 without a single hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 14, 1999 with 134 cosponsors and referred to the Agriculture, Resources, and Armed Services Committees simultaneously.

Within two weeks it was sent down to four subcommittees — Forests and Forest Health, National Parks and Public Lands, Fisheries Conservation Wildlife and Oceans, Department Operations Oversight Nutrition and Forestry, and Military Installations and Facilities — and executive comment was requested from USDA, Interior, and DOD.
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote occurred, and the action history ends in July 1999, before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
Federal logging on national forests and other public lands continued throughout, despite the bill's own findings that such programs cost taxpayers heavily.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber companies and the federal timber-sale program are better off, because clearcutting and road building on national forests, BLM land, and refuges continued uninterrupted and no citizen suits, logging bans, or end to below-cost federal timber sales followed. The Forest Service and other land agencies also avoided the mandatory-damage and open-litigation regime the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber companies and federal logging programs

for.name: Anna Eshoo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Act to Save America's Forests on July 14, 1999, with a large bloc of initial cosponsors from both the House Progressive and moderate wings.

for.name: 127 of 211 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making up the overwhelming majority of its 134 cosponsors.

for.name: 6 of 222 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including one Republican (Christopher Shays) among the original introducers.

against.name: Larry Combest
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee and its forestry subcommittee on July 23, 1999, and no markup, hearing vote, or report ever followed for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Don Young
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee and its National Parks and Public Lands and Fisheries subcommittees on July 22, 1999, and never advanced to a markup or vote.

against.name: Floyd Spence
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee and its Military Installations and Facilities subcommittee on July 27, 1999, and no action followed for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Timber industry
against.role: Forest products companies dependent on federal timber sales
against.what_they_did: Continued purchasing federal timber throughout the 106th Congress while forest-protection legislation restricting clearcutting on federal lands sat unacted-upon in committee.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 127 of 134 cosponsors were House Democrats, with 6 Republicans and 1 Independent — and every committee with jurisdiction was chaired by a Republican who never scheduled action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have banned clearcutting and even-aged logging on national forests, BLM land, refuges, and military lands and closed old-growth and roadless areas to logging, cutting off companies that depend on cheap federal timber. Its interest in continuing federal clearcutting ran directly against the public's interest in protected forests and against taxpayers, whom the bill's findings describe as subsidizing federal logging at a loss.

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation, fishing, and tourism businesses
industries.note: The bill's findings state that destruction of large-scale natural forests has already cost jobs in the fishing, hunting, tourism, recreation, and guiding industries, which would benefit from protected unfragmented forests. Their commercial interest lines up with the public's interest in intact forests.

industries.industry: Federal land-management agencies (Forest Service, BLM, Fish and Wildlife Service, Defense)
industries.note: Agencies would lose discretion over logging on the lands they manage and face mandatory citizen lawsuits with minimum damages and waived immunity, but they would also stop running below-cost timber programs that the bill's findings say drain the Treasury. The net is a real transfer of management power from agencies and courts to litigants.
